beats.lead: Every programmer's first program says the same thing
beats.note: 'Hello, world' is inseparable from Kernighan and Ritchie's 1978 C book. Kernighan had already written it six years earlier, for a language almost nobody remembers.

beats.name: Brian Kernighan
beats.role: Wrote a tutorial for a language called B, a direct predecessor to C. It included a short program with one job: print a greeting to the terminal.

beats.caption: Split into three pieces on purpose.

beats.text: B could only hold four characters at a time.
beats.note: A character constant in B was limited to four ASCII characters, so 'hello, world' had to be broken into three variables and printed one after another.

beats.lead: The version everyone knows came later
beats.text: And it had already been used for two years before the famous book.
beats.note: Kernighan reused the phrase in a 1974 Bell Labs internal memo, 'Programming in C: A Tutorial' — four years before The C Programming Language made it the standard first line of code for everyone after.

beats.line: The most copied program in computing started as a workaround.
